snip.t: Diazepam is a benzodiazepine that enhances the inhibitory action of gamma-aminobutyric acid in the central nervous system.
Multiple Sclerosis (MS): MS is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the protective covering of nerve fibers in the central nervous system.

Potential causes include genetic/chromosomal conditions, congenital brain abnormalities, prenatal exposures or infections, prematurity or perinatal complications, severe early malnutrition, central nervous system infections, traumatic brain injury and some metabolic disorders.
snip.s: Neurodevelopmental Disorders I: Autism Spectrum Disorder and Intellectual Disabi

snip.t: Central nervous system: Meninges (meningitis), brain parenchyma (tuberculoma).

Absolute contraindications to fibrinolytics include previous hemorrhagic stroke, ischemic stroke within six months, known central nervous system neoplasm or vascular malformation, recent major trauma/surgery, active internal bleeding, or suspected aortic dissection.
snip.s: Acute coronary syndrome and myocardial infarction

snip.t: Localization symptoms: Cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea (respiratory); dysuria, flank pain (urinary); photophobia, neck stiffness, confusion (central nervous system); abdominal pain, diarrhea (gastrointestinal); joint pains or rashes (rheumatologic/arboviral).
These indicate central nervous system (CNS) infections like cryptococcal meningitis, cerebral toxoplasmosis, or tuberculoma.

qs.q: A patient is diagnosed with rabies following a stray dog bite. The virus travels via retrograde axonal transport to the central nervous system. Which host cell receptor does the rabies virus glycoprotein bind to achieve entry?
o: Intercellular adhesion molecule one found on nasal mucosal endothelial cells.
CD4 molecules present on the surface of local dendritic and Langerhans cells.
Sialoglycoproteins expressed abundantly on epithelial cells of the upper airway.
Complement receptor type two expressed on circulating naive B lymphocytes.
Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors located at the neuromuscular junction synapses.
qs.e: Rabies virus binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction before retrograde axonal transport.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Virology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 35-year-old man presents with progressive neurological deterioration and hydrophobia after being bitten by a stray dog in a foreign country. What is the definitive mechanism by which the rabies virus reaches the central nervous system?
o: Hematogenous dissemination via passive movement in the lymphatic flow
Retrograde axonal transport utilizing fast motor protein machinery
Direct replication inside epineurial macrophages migrating to spinal roots
Extracellular diffusion through fascial tissue planes toward the brainstem
Infection of capillary endothelial cells leading to blood-brain barrier breakdown
qs.e: Rabies virus travels retrogradely along peripheral nerve axons to reach the central nervous system.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Microbiology II — Virology & Mycology Exam - October 30,

qs.q: A patient with an inherited urea cycle defect presents with hyperammonemia and neurological impairment. Which specific metabolic intermediate is most directly depleted in the central nervous system due to ammonia detoxification?
o: Oxaloacetate consumption via cellular transamination pathways
Malate accumulation inhibiting cytosolic malate dehydrogenase
Pyruvate diversion into peripheral tissue lactate production
Alpha-ketoglutarate depletion from the tricarboxylic acid cycle
Succinyl-CoA depletion halting cellular heme biosynthetic pathways
qs.e: Excess brain ammonia is fixed by combining with glutamate to form glutamine, depleting alpha-ketoglutarate and stalling the TCA cycle.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Clinical Biochemistry Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A pathology resident examines brain tissue under a microscope and focuses on the resident mononuclear phagocytes of the central nervous system that respond to injury. What are these specialized cells called?
o: Stellate astrocytes providing structural support to neurons
Oligodendrocytes responsible for central myelin sheath synthesis
Microglial cells acting as the primary resident macrophages
Ependymal cells lining the fluid-filled ventricular cavities
Schwann cells forming peripheral nerve insulating coverings
qs.e: Microglial cells are the resident macrophages of the central nervous system derived from primitive myeloid progenitors.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Cellular Immunology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A pathology resident examining brain tissue under a microscope focuses on the resident macrophages of the central nervous system that respond to injury and infection. What are these specialized cells designated as?
o: Oligodendroglial elements forming myelin sheaths
Perivascular dendritic cells regulating traffic
Astroglial support cells maintaining barriers
Microglial cells patrolling the neural parenchyma
Ependymal lining cells filtering cerebrospinal fluid
qs.e: Microglia are the resident mononuclear phagocytes and primary innate immune cells of the central nervous system.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Cellular Immunology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A patient with pulmonary symptoms and cerebral manifestations is found to have ectopic fluke lesions. Surgery confirms an infection with Paragonimus westermani. How did the larvae reach the central nervous system?
o: Direct swallowing of sputum containing eggs
Hematogenous spread via pulmonary veins
Ascending neural tracking along nerves
Aberrant migration through diaphragm tissues
Lymphatic drainage into thoracic duct
qs.e: Aberrant juvenile flukes can migrate through tissues and cross the diaphragm, occasionally reaching the brain instead of the lungs.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Parasitology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A trauma team is resuscitating a severely injured patient with a GCS of 7. Which intervention is indicated during the primary survey to protect the central nervous system from secondary ischemic insults?
o: Administration of high-dose intravenous corticosteroids
Insertion of a central venous catheter for glucose infusion
Immediate intubation to secure the airway
Prophylactic hyperventilation to a PaCO2 of 25 mmHg
qs.e: Patients with a GCS of 8 or less should be intubated to protect the airway and prevent hypoxia. Steroids are explicitly not recommended in head injury due to demonstrated harm in clinical trials.
qs.s: Head Injury: Assessment, Intracranial Haematomas and Management of: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following clinical features is classically categorized under the central nervous system and muscular manifestations of thyrotoxicosis?
o: Isolated systolic hypertension
Proximal myopathy
Hyperdefecation
Oligomenorrhoea
qs.e: Proximal myopathy, presenting as difficulty rising from a chair, is a CNS and muscle manifestation of thyrotoxicosis. Isolated systolic hypertension is cardiovascular, hyperdefecation is gastrointestinal, and oligomenorrhoea is reproductive.

ai.title: Central Nervous System in Paediatrics
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord, the control centre for all body functions. In low‑resource settings, infections, malnutrition and trauma are the main threats. Rapid bedside assessment and targeted investigations guide life‑saving treatment.

sections.p: The CNS comprises the brain, spinal cord and meninges. Diagnosis starts with a focused history and examination, then uses simple imaging or CSF studies when available.
b: History of fever, seizures, altered consciousness
Neuro‑deficits, papilledema, neck stiffness

t.b: Rule out meningitis or TB meningitis – CSF opening pressure, cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture, Xpert MTB/RIF

sections.p: Severity is graded by level of consciousness and focal deficits. The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is the most useful tool in children.
b: GCS 13‑15: mild
GCS 9‑12: moderate
GCS 3‑8: severe

sections.p: In East Africa, infections dominate. Malnutrition, HIV, malaria and trauma also contribute.
b: Bacterial meningitis (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae)
Tuberculous meningitis
Cryptococcal meningitis (HIV)
Malaria‑associated cerebral malaria
Traumatic brain injury
Sickle‑cell crises

sections.p: Presentation varies with age and cause. Common features include fever, seizures, vomiting, lethargy and focal neuro‑signs.
b: Seizure type: generalized tonic‑clonic, focal, febrile
Headache, neck stiffness, photophobia
Altered sensorium, vomiting, papilledema

sections.p: Use the simplest tests that answer a specific clinical question. When a test is unavailable, use clinical judgment and supportive care.

t.b: High WBC suggests bacterial infection; low Hb may indicate anaemia complicating CNS disease
Normal CT allows safe LP; abnormal CT requires neurosurgical input

sections.p: Certain signs predict poor outcome or need urgent intervention.
b: Severe headache with papilledema – raised intracranial pressure
Seizure >5 minutes – status epilepticus
Focal deficits – possible stroke or abscess
Unexplained bleeding – consider haemorrhagic stroke

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, support vital functions and monitor for complications. Drug choice favours safety and availability.
b: Empiric antibiotics for bacterial meningitis: ceftriaxone + ampicillin (or cefotaxime + ampicillin)
Anti‑TB therapy: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol
Antifungals for cryptococcal meningitis: amphotericin B + flucytosine (if available)
Antimalarials: artesunate for cerebral malaria
Supportive care: maintain airway, oxygen, fluids, glucose, seizure control with phenobarbitone or phenytoin

sections.p: Early discharge planning, vaccination and community education reduce recurrence.
b: Ensure completion of full anti‑TB course
Vaccinate against Hib and pneumococcus
Educate caregivers on early signs of meningitis
Screen for HIV and provide ART

sections.p: Several conditions mimic CNS disease; recognising differences is key.
b: Febrile seizures – isolated seizure, no focal deficits
Sepsis with encephalopathy – diffuse, no focal signs
Traumatic brain injury – history of injury, focal deficits

sections.p: Some investigations may give false negatives or positives in low‑resource settings.
b: CSF glucose can be normal in TB meningitis if glucose is low systemically
Xpert MTB/RIF may miss paucibacillary TB
Rapid malaria tests may miss low parasitaemia

faq.q: Why is a lumbar puncture contraindicated in raised intracranial pressure?
faq.a: It can cause brain herniation by suddenly lowering CSF pressure.

faq.q: What is the first drug to give in suspected bacterial meningitis?
faq.a: Empiric ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) plus ampicillin to cover common organisms.

faq.q: How do you differentiate tuberculous meningitis from bacterial meningitis clinically?
faq.a: TB meningitis is slower, with chronic fever, cranial nerve palsies and a lymphocytic CSF; bacterial meningitis is acute with neutrophilic CSF and high opening pressure.

exam: A 6‑year‑old presents with fever, vomiting and a stiff neck. What is the first investigation you would do and why? — LP after normal CT to rule out meningitis, but only if no signs of raised ICP. A child with altered consciousness and a positive malaria rapid test. What is the next step? — Immediate artesunate and supportive care; do not delay for imaging. A 3‑year‑old with seizures and a history of sickle cell disease. What is the most likely cause and first treatment? — Acu
